title: The Vow at Ambika's Temple
subtitle: Rukmini's silent prayer as her wedding dawns
story:
A single night lay between Rukmini and her wedding, and the man she had chosen had not come. She was the princess of Vidarbha, daughter of King Bhishmaka of Kundina, and her family had promised her hand to Shishupala, prince of Chedi. Rukmini had chosen differently. She had sent a trusted brahmana to Dwaraka, to Krishna, with a message: come before the wedding, and carry me away. The wedding was one night away. Krishna had not come.

Her mind, which had been with Krishna ever since her message went out, would not rest. One night was all that remained, and she was a girl of small fortune — what if the flawless one found something in her to blame? Even the gods seemed set against her: the maker of her birth had never favored her, and the great god Shiva had not blessed her hope. Tears came while she prayed, with everything in her, that Krishna alone would be her husband.

Then, at last, the brahmana came back. The same messenger she had sent to Dwaraka returned, sent back now by Krishna himself, his face bright with a joy that lifted her heart before he spoke a word: Krishna had come. He had reached Vidarbha. He was here.

News travels fast in a wedding city. Bhishmaka heard that Krishna had arrived among the gathered kings, and he offered him the madhuparka — the honeyed welcome kept for honored guests — with fresh garments, and made a splendid residence ready for him. And the people of Vidarbha, seeing Krishna walk among them, said openly what everyone felt: "Rukmini deserves to be his wife, and no other. What good deed did we do, that the maker of the three worlds should be pleased with us?" Love bound the whole city; they spoke of nothing else.

Then came the day of the procession of the family goddess — the very day Rukmini's message had pointed to. Under a vow of silence, she went out on foot to the temple of Ambika, her mothers and her companions all around her. Thousands of women followed with offerings in their hands; singers sang and musicians played; and the whole city poured out to watch the bride go to the goddess's shrine.

At the shrine she washed her hands and her feet. The elderly brahmana women who knew the rites worshipped the goddess with water, perfume, unbroken rice, incense, fresh garments, garlands, and ornaments, and the married women of the household joined them in the worship. Then they gave Rukmini the remainder of the offerings and spoke their blessings over her. And Rukmini, bowing before the goddess, prayed the one prayer she had carried in her heart across all those miles: that Krishna alone would be her husband. "Grant this," she breathed.

She rose, set aside her vow of silence, and came out of Ambika's temple. And the gathered heroes who saw her — slim-waisted, her face bright with earrings, her smile pure — stood struck silent, struck with love, as though the goddess's own enchantment had stepped out into the daylight.

Only one man in all that crowd did not stare. Krishna had come, as she had asked him to. And the procession that was to have delivered her to Shishupala's wedding was about to deliver her to Krishna instead.
reflection: Rukmini's prayer at the temple is both worship and the final move of her own plan: the procession she had described in her message is what brings her out of the inner apartments, into the open, where Krishna can reach her. The goddess is asked to bless what the princess has already resolved.
next_story_tease: Beyond the temple door, the hour she had written to him about had come.
hero_scene: Rukmini kneeling in silent prayer before the image of Ambika in the incense-filled shrine, her hands joined, her mothers and friends around her, the lamp of the goddess lighting her bowed head as the brahmana women chant blessings.
